title: Same demand rise, different jobs

predict.q: Demand rises by the same amount for two jobs: **warehouse pickers** (elastic supply) and **airline pilots** (inelastic supply in the short run). Each starts at wage **20**, **1,000** workers. Which job sees the bigger rise in its wage?

options.s: Pickers, because their supply is elastic.
options.fb: Elastic supply means many extra workers come forward, so the wage needs to rise only a little (20 → 22).

options.s: Pilots, because their supply is inelastic.
options.fb: Few extra pilots can come forward, so the wage does the adjusting: 20 → 28 (+40%), against 20 → 22 for pickers.

options.s: Both the same, because the demand rise is the same.
options.fb: The same demand shift splits differently between wage and jobs, depending on the slope of supply.

options.s: Neither: wages stay at 20, and only employment rises.
options.fb: With an upward-sloping supply curve, more workers come forward only at a higher wage.

task: Move the demand slider to 10, then switch the supply setting between elastic and inelastic, and watch the wage and employment.

target.do: Move the demand slider to 10 (try both supply settings), then press Check.

takeaway: Inelastic supply → most of a demand rise goes into **higher wages**; elastic supply → mostly **more jobs**.
